courses.title: Grassroots Democracy: Leadership and Power - HONORS
courses.description: This course provides both applied and theoretical training for students of social justice. It serves as a multidisciplinary exploration of social change and popular democratic action, with a specific focus on understanding the meaning and development of political power in modern democracies. This course will explore gender and race-sensitive approaches to leadership style, the utilization of institutional and mass forums for civic engagement, strategies for mass recruitment and mobilization, consciousness development, democratic ethics, and strategic and tactical action. Furthermore, as an honors course, students are expected to complete additional assignments aimed at gaining deeper insight into the issues that are raised.

courses.title: Comparative Politics
courses.description: This course offers a comparative analysis of various political systems, examining their historical development, political institutions, societal structures, cultural influences, economic systems, political processes, and public policies. It also explores the environmental conditions in which these systems operate and evaluates the broader consequences they produce.

courses.title: Introduction to Political Thought and Theory
courses.description: This course provides a comprehensive survey of the field of political theory, focusing on how to interpret, discuss, critique, debate, and write about both classical and contemporary political thought and theory. It examines traditional approaches alongside more current paradigms, especially those that address the perspectives of constituent groups who have traditionally been excluded from mainstream political discourse. Throughout this course, students will develop the ability to think and engage critically with both classical and modern political issues, including topics such as the balance between individual and community rights, freedom, equality, and distributional justice. Additionally, students will explore issues like environmental sustainability, generational equity, the "rights" of nature and non-human life, power, sovereignty, and the state, among others.

courses.title: Introduction to Administration of Justice
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the characteristics of the criminal justice system in the United States. The content focuses on examining crime measurement, theoretical explanations of crime, response to crime, components of the system, and current challenges to the system. It also examines the evolution of the principles and approaches utilized by the justice system in crime control and the evolving forces that have shaped those principles and approaches. The justice component structures and processes are examined in a cross-cultural context, emphasizing the relationship and partnership between the police and the diverse community populations. Students are introduced to the origins and development of criminal law, the legal process, sentencing, and incarceration policies.

courses.title: Grassroots Democracy: Race, Politics and the American Promise
courses.description: This course offers both applied and theoretical learning for students of social justice. It will delve into an examination of race, culture, and contradictions inherent in the ideal of the American Dream through a comparative analysis of American experiences of migration. Special focus will be placed on the historical experiences of European immigrants, African Americans, Mexican Americans, and Asian Americans. Additionally, the course will address contemporary social and cultural implications of the migration process. Employing a multidisciplinary social science approach, the course will pay attention to issues of race, ethnicity, gender, class, and ecology. Furthermore, it will explore the role of the state, particularly in terms of policy, in shaping the processes of migration and immigration.

courses.title: Grassroots Democracy: Social Movements Since the 1960s
courses.description: This course offers both applied and theoretical learning for students of social justice, serving as a comparative survey of protest movements since the 1960s. It provides an introductory, comparative, and interdisciplinary study of social and political struggles among Mexican American, African American, Asian American, and white working-class communities from 1960 to the present day. Throughout the course, there is a focus on tracing the development of these protest movements in response to various forms of inequality, including racial, class, gender, ecological, and political disparities within the context of U.S. politics and history. Moreover, the course critically examines both internal and external factors contributing to the rise and fall of social and political movements. Special attention is given to the intersectionality of ecology, gender, race, ethnicity, culture, class, and sexual orientation within contemporary U.S. politics.

It provides an introductory, comparative, and interdisciplinary study of social and political struggles among Mexican American, African American, Asian American, and white working-class communities from 1960 to the present day. Throughout the course, there is a focus on tracing the development of these protest movements in response to various forms of inequality, including racial, class, gender, ecological, and political disparities within the context of U.S. politics and history. Moreover, the course critically examines both internal and external factors contributing to the rise and fall of social and political movements. Special attention is given to the intersectionality of ecology, gender, race, ethnicity, culture, class, and sexual orientation within contemporary U.S. politics.

courses.student_learning_outcomes: Investigate and identify key events and experiences of major social protest movements since the 1960's. Identify, appraise, and compare factors leading to the development of social protest consciousness in social protest movements since the 1960's with specific attention to issues of ethnicity, race, class, ecology and gender. Demonstrate the capacity to participate effectively in political processes and techniques common to social movements.

courses.title: Grassroots Democracy: Leadership and Power
courses.description: This course provides both applied and theoretical training for students of social justice. It serves as a multidisciplinary exploration of social change and popular democratic action, with a specific focus on understanding the meaning and development of political power in modern democracies. This course will explore gender and race-sensitive approaches to leadership style, the utilization of institutional and mass forums for civic engagement, strategies for mass recruitment and mobilization, consciousness development, democratic ethics, and strategic and tactical action.

courses.title: Introduction to Statistics for the Behavioral and Social Sciences
courses.description: This course is an introduction to statistics through applied application within government, politics, and social and behavioral sciences. Students will explore concepts such as central tendency, variability, probability, correlation, and significance tests and test hypotheses through real-life applications. Students will understand and demonstrate the key concepts of descriptive and inferential statistics and methods for scientific analysis as applied within the fields of political science, social science, and behavioral science.
courses.prerequisites: Intermediate algebra or equivalent (or higher), or appropriate placement beyond intermediate algebra.

metadata.Transferability: Transferable to both UC and CSU
metadata.Prerequisite(s): Intermediate algebra or equivalent (or higher), or appropriate placement beyond intermediate algebra.
metadata.Student Learning Outcomes: Evaluate and analyze the fundamental concepts of descriptive and inferential statistics as well as the major assumptions and methods of scientific analysis. Evaluate and apply various measurement concepts appropriate to different types of research data. Graph and interpret basic frequency distributions, calculate and explain measures of central tendency and variability. Calculate and test the basic properties of the normal curve and standard scores. Calculate and run linear regression, correlations, random sampling and probability analyses. Conduct hypothesis testing for the three primary varieties of T-tests to analysis of variance.
